messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: Some questions about log Gaussian Cox processes

- inla.spde.query does generate a sample from a zero-mean Gaussian random field.  For the parameters given, the range of the random field is around 5.5, so the field is essentially intrinsic on the domain.  This explains the all positive (or all negative) samples.  If you make kappa smaller, this will be better.

- simulate_lgcp  uses exp(weights), so it doesn't rely on weights being positive.

/Dan

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: Some questions about log Gaussian Cox processes
parts:
Hi,
some further explanations; tau is a rescaling parameter that controls the variance of the model, and kappa controls the spatial correlation range.  On R^2, with alpha=2 in the SPDE model, the relations are
  variance = 1/(2*pi*kappa^2*tau^2)
and
  range = sqrt(8)/kappa

In the code you ran, the domain has width 1, so the spatial correlation range, sqrt(8)/0.5 = 4*sqrt(2), is larger than the size of the domain.  This gives a high probability that the "observed" part of the field will lie entirely above or entirely below zero.  This effect is further exaggerated by the boundary conditions (normal derivatives equal to zero).  The classical intrinsic models are defined by kappa=0, which gives "infinite spatial correlation range", but the range 4*sqrt(2) obtained for kappa=0.5 is already so much larger than the domain that the practical effects will be similar.

In summary, if you run the code several times, the samples generated by inla.spde.query should equally often be above zeros and below zero.

I haven't added the one-dimensional SDE models to the interface yet, but they will appear in the not-too-distant future...

/Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: Some questions about log Gaussian Cox processes
parts:
Further comment:

I sense a small confusion about "mean","expectation" and "average":
The models have "expectation zero" (which is often written as "mean zero") which is not to be confused with "empirical average zero for a single realisation".  If you produce many samples, the overall average will tend to the expectation, but the average in a single realisation need not be close to the expectation.

/Finn

Hello, 
         I've found something misleading in page 8 in Simpson et al. It occurred in line #3 in the second paragraph, namely,
                                 \alpha = (\tilde{alpha}, "0").

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: Some questions about log Gaussian Cox processes
parts:
Yes.  That's an unfortunate typo.  In (7), the first alpha should not be there, but the one in the exponential should be there and should be equal to zero.  The relationship (7) is "true" in the sense that if you take logarithms and define log(0) = 0, then (7) and (6) are equivalent.  This is related to the way this model needs to be implemented in INLA.

There is a second typo: \eta should be the exponential of (\mm{z}^T\mm{A}_1^T,\mm{z}^T\mm{A}_2^T)^T.

Thanks for pointing that out.

Best wishes,

Dan
